title: Rank-Refined Quantum-Behaved Particle Swarm Optimization for Quantum Molecular Generation
authors: Sing-Yun Wu, Sheng Yun Wu, I-Min Chiang, Tai-Yue Li
abstract: This work proposes Rank-Refined Quantum-Behaved Particle Swarm Optimization (RR-QPSO) for high-dimensional parameter search in Quantum Molecular Generation (QMG). RR-QPSO targets the optimization bottleneck caused by expensive objective evaluations, where each candidate parameter vector requires stochastic circuit sampling, bitstring decoding, and molecular evaluation. The method provides a population-based alternative to Bayesian optimization (BO), combining Sobol-based initialization, a rank-refined mean-best update, and fitness-guided refinement based on validity and uniqueness. Experiments use the 9-heavy-atom QMG benchmark with a 134-parameter, 20-qubit CUDA-Q circuit and particle evaluations parallelized across 8 NVIDIA V100 GPUs. With M=64 particles and T=150 iterations, RR-QPSO reaches VxU = 0.930; increasing the swarm size to M=128 further improves the product to 0.942, compared with 0.902 for BO under the same protocol. A multi-objective extension targeting HBA=4 and HBD=3 further shows that RR-QPSO can guide molecular properties while preserving a higher validity--uniqueness product than BO. These results suggest that optimizer-level design can improve QMG without modifying the chemistry-inspired circuit or molecular decoding pipeline.
summary: The paper proposes a novel optimization algorithm, RR-QPSO, to overcome the computational bottleneck in Quantum Molecular Generation (QMG). This method uses advanced swarm intelligence techniques to efficiently search high-dimensional parameter spaces governing quantum circuits. The results demonstrate that this optimizer design significantly improves molecular quality metrics compared to existing methods like Bayesian Optimization.
main_problem: The primary challenge is optimizing parameters for Quantum Molecular Generation (QMG) due to an expensive objective evaluation bottleneck involving stochastic circuit sampling.
main_result: The proposed RR-QPSO significantly outperforms Bayesian Optimization on the 9-heavy-atom QMG benchmark, achieving a higher validity–uniqueness product (up to 0.942 vs 0.902).
method: The authors introduce Rank-Refined Quantum-Behaved Particle Swarm Optimization (RR-QPSO), which uses Sobol initialization and rank-refined mean-best updates as a population-based alternative to BO.
model_or_system: The work focuses on QMG, a process that generates molecules using a chemistry-inspired dynamic quantum circuit parameterized by $\theta$ within a 20-qubit system for the 9-heavy-atom benchmark.
key_observables: Validity–Uniqueness product ($V \times U$), Validity ($V$), Uniqueness ($U$), mean HBA, and mean HBD.
important_parameters: Circuit parameters $D=134$, Swarm size $M$ (e.g., 64 or 128), Iterations $T=150$.
main_assumptions: The objective function is noisy and expensive to evaluate because it relies on finite circuit samples from stochastic sampling.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the RR-QPSO workflow: Sobol sampling $\rightarrow$ Parallel QMG Evaluation (on multiple GPUs) $\rightarrow$ Fitness Calculation ($F=V \times U$) $\rightarrow$ RR-QPSO Update. Other figures compare performance against BO and show scaling with particle count.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the optimization bottleneck in QMG, proposes RR-QPSO as a superior population-based optimizer over BO, details its components (Sobol initialization, rank refinement), validates it on the 9-heavy-atom benchmark across varying swarm sizes, and extends to multi-objective property guidance.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the computational feasibility of quantum chemistry simulations by improving the optimization layer used to guide molecular structure generation from quantum circuits.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. RR-QPSO workflow for QMG parameter optimization. Sobol sampling initializes a swarm of M candidate parameter vectors, which are evaluated through QMG circuit sampling, bitstring decoding, molecular graph generation, and fitness computation. The independent particle evaluations are distributed across K GPUs, and the resulting scores are used to update the RR-QPSO swarm.

Fig. 2. Optimizer performance comparison on the 9-heavy-atom QMG benchmark. The bars report validity, uniqueness, and their product. QPSO- based runs use M = 64 particles, T = 150 iterations, and 5000-shot molecular evaluation. RR-QPSO gives the highest validity–uniqueness product in this experimental setting.
Fig. 3. Effect of particle count on RR-QPSO convergence. Curves show the best validity–uniqueness product observed up to each iteration for different swarm sizes M. The dashed line indicates BO.

Fig. 4. Multi-objective optimization targeting HBA = 4 and HBD = 3. BO and RR-QPSO are evaluated under the same scalarized target-property objective. RR-QPSO retains a higher validity–uniqueness product while keeping the generated molecules close to the target HBA and HBD region in this scalarized setting.
